strengths: Clear motivation addressing genuine limitations (computational overhead, overconfidence) of self-evaluation methods on unverifiable tasks
Substantial computational efficiency gains (0.1%-5% of self-evaluation cost) with significant practical implications
Comprehensive experimental validation across 6 model architectures and multiple tasks with both lexical and semantic metrics
Rigorous ablation studies examining clustering, embedding models, hyperparameters, and alternative training paradigms (GRPO)
Clever flipped-SV validation experiment to distinguish real signal from spurious rewards
Elegant simplicity—straightforward extension of majority voting to open-ended tasks through semantic soft-matching
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation details and promised code release
Solid out-of-distribution generalization results showing benefits transfer to unseen WMT datasets
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: semantic similarity for consensus, clustering borrowed from EMPO, DPO standard—contribution feels incremental
Inconsistent and mixed empirical results: Llama-3B consistently underperforms; method not clearly superior across settings, sometimes only 'on par' with baselines
Model-dependent behavior undermines generality: clustering necessity varies by model quality; different hyperparameter requirements per model with limited guidance on when method applies
Narrow task scope: only translation and summarization evaluated (both similar text-generation tasks); no reasoning tasks; generalization to other open-ended tasks unclear

Weak baseline implementations: Self-judging and entropy minimization produce many 'NA' failures suggesting suboptimal tuning; hard to assess if SVSI is truly superior or baselines are poorly configured
Incomplete spurious reward validation: flipped-SV shows some cases still outperform base model, indicating residual spurious improvements not fully accounted for
Unexamined core assumptions: semantic consensus may not correlate with quality; no empirical validation that high voting scores correspond to better outputs; lack of manual evaluation
Limited GRPO extensibility: Section 4.5 shows SVSI-G less stable than EMPO, suggesting DPO's robustness is method-specific, limiting general applicability
Missing error analysis and insights into failure modes, particularly why performance varies dramatically across models (e.g., Llama-3B struggles)
Hyperparameter sensitivity contradicts 'lightweight' claims: temperature, sampling size, and clustering parameters all require tuning; practical applicability to new tasks/models unclear

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a real gap: majority voting inapplicable to open-ended tasks, self-evaluation methods expensive and biased
Significant computational efficiency gains (0.1-5% of baseline costs), with clear practical value for deployment
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 models, 6 datasets, multiple lexical and semantic metrics with extensive ablations
Strong validation methodology including flipped-SV experiment that convincingly demonstrates meaningful signals beyond spurious rewards
Consistent improvements across most settings with better stability than baselines, avoiding severe degradation
Sound technical approach with thorough hyperparameter studies and sensitivity analyses
Excellent reproducibility: code released, public datasets, detailed appendices with implementation details
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: semantic matching via embeddings is a natural, straightforward extension of majority voting rather than a fundamentally new insight
Inconsistent performance across models, particularly Llama-3B underperformance, with limited explanation of failure modes and model-specific requirements
Restricted task evaluation to two related language generation tasks (translation, summarization); generalization to other open-ended tasks remains unclear
Linguistic diversity reduction (Appendix H) raises model collapse concerns insufficiently addressed; higher temperature workaround is not a fundamental solution
Lack of theoretical justification for why semantic consensus among model-generated responses indicates correctness; potential failure mode of converged-upon errors unexplored
Clustering dependency introduces complexity and hyperparameter tuning; different models require different strategies, undermining simplicity claims
Limited baseline comparisons: self-judging baseline appears weak; missing comparisons to quality estimation models and other consensus methods
Embedding model sensitivity (Table 2) suggests fragility for smaller models; cross-encoders insufficiently evaluated
GRPO integration shows stability issues (Section 4.5) requiring discretization, limiting claimed broad applicability across training paradigms
Insufficient qualitative error analysis: no case studies or examples showing what improvements semantic voting captures or which error types it corrects
Lack of statistical rigor: no significance tests, confidence intervals, or consistency of improvements across multiple runs for main results
Many 'NA' entries in Table 1 reduce scope of main comparisons; evaluation subsets (1,000 samples) may limit reliability of summarization results

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Articulates genuine limitation that majority voting requires exact matching while self-evaluation methods are computationally expensive and prone to overconfidence bias
Dramatic computational efficiency gains: Reduces overhead to 0.1-5% of self-evaluation baselines, which is practically significant for scaling to larger models

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tested on 6 diverse models (Llama, Qwen) across 6 datasets (4 translation, 2 summarization) with both lexical and semantic metrics, plus extensive ablations and hyperparameter studies

Rigorous validation methodology: Flipped-SV experiment (Figure 4) elegantly verifies that semantic voting captures meaningful signals rather than spurious rewards; performance degradation is proportional to gains
Excellent reproducibility: Code promised for release, detailed implementation details, hyperparameters well-specified, public datasets used, and prompt templates provided
Thoughtful design choices: Clustering-based filtering is well-motivated for handling outliers, with good ablation analysis showing necessity varies by model capacity
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Combines existing techniques (sentence embeddings, clustering, DPO) in straightforward manner; main insight of soft vs. hard matching is relatively obvious

Mixed performance against baselines: Figure 2 and Table 1 show SVSI does not consistently outperform self-evaluation methods; underperforms notably on Llama-3B; many improvements are marginal; no statistical significance testing
Reduced linguistic diversity: Table 6 shows non-trivial semantic diversity reduction (e.g., RSMD 33.20→29.66 on CNN/DailyMail); concern is dismissed rather than adequately addressed
Limited task scope: Only translation and summarization tested despite broad evaluation; these are relatively structured tasks; minimal evaluation on creative generation tasks

Weak theoretical justification: No principled explanation for why semantic consensus via embeddings should predict task quality; connection between embedding similarity and correctness is assumed rather than justified
GRPO extensibility concerns: SVSI-G shows notable instability with high variance; suggests method may not generalize well beyond DPO, limiting broader applicability

Hyperparameter sensitivity and tuning complexity: Despite simplicity claims, Figures 7-8 show non-trivial sensitivity to temperature, sampling size, and clustering parameters; no analysis of tuning cost

Embedding model analysis incomplete: Section 4.8 claims similar performance but shows DeBERTa-v3 notable drop on Llama-1B; limited analysis of why embedding quality appears less critical than expected
Clustered results present mixed evidence: Ablation (Figure 6) shows clustering necessity varies with model capacity, suggesting method effectiveness is model-dependent; adds engineering complexity
Dataset size limitations: CNN/DailyMail and PubMed use only 1,000 samples; translation uses full datasets, creating inconsistent evaluation; limits confidence in summarization results
